message.content: {"results":[{"author":"Nancy Sherman","year":"1989","title":"The Fabric of Character: Aristotle’s Theory of Virtue","venue":"Oxford: Clarendon Press","url":"https://archive.org/details/fabricofcharacte0000sher","verbatim_quotation":"“Unlike the habituation that belongs to technē, which aims at the reliable production of an external product according to a pre‑given pattern, ethical habituation aims at shaping the agent’s praxis itself.  It is not merely the acquisition of a routine, but the internalization of reasons for acting; it depends upon the learner’s gradually coming to see, through doing, why certain responses are called for here and now.  In this way habituation in virtue is from the start informed by practical reason and directed toward the refinement of emotional comportment.”","page_anchor":"pp. 157–159","why_relevant":"Sherman explicitly contrasts technē‑like habituation, oriented to external products, with the praxis‑oriented habituation of character, and she stresses that the latter involves the agent’s grasp of reasons and perception of particulars, thereby grounding the shaping and regulation of emotions in Aristotle’s ethics."},{"author":"Nancy Sherman","year":"1990","title":"Review of Nancy Sherman, The Fabric of Character: Aristotle’s Theory of Virtue","venue":"Ethics 100(4)","url":"https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/pdf/10.1086/293245","verbatim_quotation":"“Sherman is persuasive that habituation is more rational and reflective and less mechanical for Aristotle than it has often been represented as being (pp. 157–99).  Habituation in virtue is not the inculcation of a craftlike routine but a process in which the learner acquires the capacity to deliberate well about what is to be done, to perceive situations as calling for certain emotional responses, and to act for the sake of the noble.”","page_anchor":"p. 894","why_relevant":"This review distills Sherman’s central claim that Aristotelian habituation is not technē‑like ‘mechanical training’ but intrinsically practical‑rational, shaping how agents perceive situations and respond emotionally in praxis."},{"author":"Pierre Aubenque","year":"1963","title":"La prudence chez Aristote","venue":"Paris: Presses Universitaires de France","url":"https://archive.org/details/trent_0116301986695","verbatim_quotation":"« Il faut distinguer la prudence des autres vertus, en particulier morales, par une différence : la vertu morale est une disposition pratique concernant le choix, la prudence est une disposition pratique concernant la règle du choix (disposition à agir accompagnée de la règle, EN, VI, 5).  Il s’agit ici, non plus de la rectitude de l’action mais de la justice du critère.  Ainsi la justice abstraite aura besoin d’être rectifiée par la vertu d’équité.  […] L’homme équitable devra posséder la vertu de la prudence, qui lui permettra chaque fois de définir la norme, pour l’appliquer à son domaine. »","page_anchor":"pp. 117–118 (chap. II, §1)","why_relevant":"Aubenque’s analysis of phronēsis as a disposition concerning the ‘rule of choice’ clarifies how praxis (not technē) involves context‑sensitive norm‑definition; this distinction underlies his claim that ethical action and affect must be guided by prudential judgment rather than craftlike routine."},{"author":"Pierre Aubenque","year":"1963","title":"La prudence chez Aristote","venue":"Paris: Presses Universitaires de France","url":"https://archive.org/details/trent_0116301986695","verbatim_quotation":"« La prudence est donc comme l’expérience, elle ne se transmet pas.  Il faut du temps pour devenir prudent.  Ne pas confondre le prudent et l’habile.  Habileté = capacité à réaliser aisément les fins, c’est‑à‑dire, une fin étant donnée, de combiner les moyens les plus efficaces (EN, VI, 13).  […] La fonction de la prudence n’est possible que dans un horizon plus universel : ce par quoi une situation en général est possible […] la prudence se meut dans le domaine du contingent. »","page_anchor":"pp. 143–145 (chap. II, §3)","why_relevant":"Here Aubenque sharply distinguishes phronēsis from mere ‘habileté’ (a technē‑like skill in means–end calculation) and stresses its experiential, contingent, praxis‑oriented character; this is crucial for explaining why genuine ethical habituation in Aristotle cannot be reduced to technē and how it shapes the agent’s comportment in concrete situations, including emotional responses."},{"author":"Jean‑Robert Armogathe (Académie des Sciences Morales et Politiques, drawing on Aristotle and Aubenque)","year":"2007","title":"La prudence","venue":"Séance de l’Académie des Sciences Morales et Politiques, 19 octobre 2007","url":"https://academiesciencesmoralesetpolitiques.fr/wp-content/uploads/2018/09/2007_10_19_prudence.pdf","verbatim_quotation":"« L’un des caractères majeurs de la praxis est que son objet n’est pas le nécessaire et l’éternel, mais le contingent et le transitoire : “Ce qui se déploie dans le champ des actions et des choses utiles n’a rien de fixe.”  La vertu qui s’exerce proprement dans ce champ pratique, c’est la prudence. […] La phronèsis […] opère la synthèse du désir et de la raison pour régir la praxis. »","page_anchor":"pp. 8–10","why_relevant":"This contemporary synthesis, indebted to Aubenque, emphasizes the specifically praxis‑oriented field of phronēsis (the contingent) and its role in synthesizing desire and reason; it therefore helps articulate how Aristotelian habituation, when governed by phronēsis rather than technē, grounds and integrates emotional comportment in action."}]}
